title: Responsive, mobile-first design
intro: A responsive website adapts to the space available instead of assuming that every visitor has the same screen. In this lesson you will build layouts that start with small screens and progressively enhance themselves as more space becomes available.
body:
## Why responsive design matters People can visit the same website from a large desktop monitor, a laptop, a tablet, or a phone held vertically. The available space can vary dramatically, and users should not have to zoom, scroll sideways, or fight with tiny controls to use your interface. Phones are an especially important part of modern web traffic. Even when your own audience eventually turns out to use desktop computers more often, you should not assume that a desktop layout will automatically work on a phone. Responsive design means that the layout responds to the available space. A useful way to think about it is: ~~~text Small screen ↓ Simple single-column layout ↓ More available space ↓ Additional columns and larger spacing ↓ Large screen ↓ Full desktop layout ~~~ The goal is not to make a separate website for every device. You normally build one page that can adapt to many viewport sizes. --- ## The viewport meta tag One of the most important lines in a responsive HTML document is: ~~~html ~~~ The **viewport** is the area of the browser in which your webpage is displayed. `width=device-width` tells the browser to use the device's actual CSS viewport width. `initial-scale=1` tells the browser to display the page at its normal initial scale rather than automatically zooming it out. Without this tag, mobile browsers historically tried to make desktop-oriented pages fit by pretending that the page was much wider than the physical screen. The result can be confusing: your CSS may appear to have a large amount of horizontal space even though the phone is physically much narrower. That can make a page designed with media queries behave unexpectedly. For modern responsive pages, put the viewport tag inside ``: ~~~html Responsive page ~~~ It is a small line with a very large effect. --- ## Fixed layouts versus fluid layouts A common beginner mistake is to give major elements fixed widths everywhere. For example: ~~~css .container { width: 1200px; } ~~~ This might look fine on a large desktop screen. On a phone, however, a 1200-pixel container cannot fit naturally into a viewport that is only a few hundred CSS pixels wide. A more flexible approach is: ~~~css .container { width: 100%; max-width: 1200px; margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: 1rem; } ~~~ Now the container can shrink when the screen becomes smaller, but it stops growing after reaching `1200px`. This combination is extremely common: - `width: 100%` lets the element use available space. - `max-width` prevents content from becoming excessively wide. - `margin-inline: auto` centres the container when there is extra horizontal space. - `rem` values provide scalable spacing. You can also use percentages for fluid dimensions: ~~~css .sidebar { width: 30%; } .content { width: 70%; } ~~~ However, percentages are not automatically the right solution for every layout. Flexbox and Grid usually provide better tools for distributing space between components. --- ## Fluid images Images can also cause horizontal overflow if they are larger than their container. A simple defensive rule is: ~~~css img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } ~~~ `max-width: 100%` means an image should not become wider than its containing block. `height: auto` preserves the image's aspect ratio when its width changes. For example, if a 1200-pixel-wide image is displayed inside a 350-pixel container, the browser can scale it down instead of forcing the page to become wider than the screen. ### Responsive images with srcset Sometimes you can do more than simply scale one large image down. The `srcset` attribute lets you provide multiple image files at different resolutions: ~~~html ~~~ The browser can use this information to choose a suitable resource for the current display size and device characteristics. You do not need `srcset` for every small image on every page, but it becomes useful when image performance matters, especially for large photographs. --- ## Mobile-first CSS Responsive CSS is often easier to maintain when you start with the smallest practical layout. ~~~widget breakpoints ~~~ This approach is called **mobile-first design**. Instead of starting with a complicated desktop layout and trying to undo it on smaller screens, you define the simple layout first and add enhancements as the viewport gets wider. For example: ~~~css .columns { display: block; } @media (min-width: 768px) { .columns { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 2rem; } } ~~~ The base rule works on small screens. Once the viewport reaches the breakpoint, the second rule creates two columns. This direction is important. You are effectively saying: ~~~text Default: one column ↓ more available space min-width breakpoint: two columns ~~~ ### Why min-width? A mobile-first stylesheet commonly uses `min-width` media queries because the base CSS represents the smallest layout and larger viewports progressively add capabilities. You can also use `max-width` media queries, and they are not inherently wrong. They are simply less aligned with the mobile-first approach when used as the main structure of the stylesheet. --- ## Choose breakpoints based on content You may hear numbers such as `640px`, `768px`, `1024px`, and `1280px` described as mobile, tablet, and desktop breakpoints. These values can be useful starting points, but you should not blindly design around specific devices. Instead, ask when the content needs more space. Imagine a navigation menu: ~~~text [Logo] [Home] [Projects] [Contact] ↓ Links no longer fit comfortably ↓ Add a breakpoint ↓ Use the larger layout ~~~ The breakpoint should exist because your content needs it, not because someone told you that a particular phone has a particular screen width. This makes your layout more resilient when new devices appear. --- ## Fluid typography with clamp() Responsive layouts do not only need flexible widths. Text can also adapt. ~~~diagram {"type": "layers", "title": "clamp(min, preferred, max)", "caption": "The font size follows the viewport but never leaves the safe range.", "layers": [{"label": "min", "sub": "1.75rem on small phones", "items": ["≈ 28px"]}, {"label": "preferred", "sub": "grows with the screen", "items": ["4vw + 1rem"], "highlight": true}, {"label": "max", "sub": "3rem on wide desktops", "items": ["≈ 48px"]}]} ~~~ CSS provides `clamp()` for this purpose: ~~~css h1 { font-size: clamp(2rem, 5vw, 4rem); } ~~~ The three values mean: - Minimum value: `2rem` - Preferred flexible value: `5vw` - Maximum value: `4rem` The browser chooses a value between the minimum and maximum based on the viewport. This can produce smoother scaling than changing the font size abruptly at several breakpoints. You can use `clamp()` for headings, spacing, and other dimensions where gradual scaling makes sense. Do not make everything fluid simply because you can. Predictability is also valuable. Fixed or breakpoint-based values are often perfectly appropriate for controls and component internals. --- ## Touch targets and readable text Responsive design is not only about making things fit. A layout can technically fit on a phone while still being frustrating to use. Interactive controls should have enough physical area to tap comfortably. A useful practical target is around **44 CSS pixels or more** for touch targets. For example: ~~~css button, a.button { min-height: 44px; padding-inline: 1rem; } ~~~ The exact size depends on the design, but tiny links packed closely together are difficult to use on touch screens. Readable text also matters. Extremely long lines are tiring to read, especially on large screens. A common approach is to limit the width of text-heavy content: ~~~css .article { max-width: 70ch; } ~~~ `ch` is a unit related to the width of the `0` character in the element's font. It can be useful for controlling line length in articles and documentation. Responsive design therefore has several goals: - Avoid horizontal scrolling. - Keep controls easy to tap. - Keep text readable. - Let images scale safely. - Use available space efficiently. --- ## A complete before-and-after example Imagine a page with a sidebar and main content. A desktop-only version might look like this: ~~~css .container { width: 1200px; margin: 0 auto; } .columns { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 300px 900px; gap: 20px; } ~~~ This assumes that there is enough horizontal space for exactly those dimensions. A phone cannot comfortably accommodate a 1200-pixel fixed container. A mobile-first version starts with a simple stack: ~~~css .container { width: 100%; max-width: 1200px; margin-inline: auto; padding-inline: 1rem; } .columns { display: block; } @media (min-width: 768px) { .columns { display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(200px, 300px) 1fr; gap: 2rem; } } ~~~ The HTML does not need to change between the layouts: ~~~html
Sidebar content
Main content
~~~ On a small screen, the content appears as a vertical sequence: ~~~text +-------------------+ | Sidebar | +-------------------+ | Main content | | | +-------------------+ ~~~ On a wider screen, the same HTML becomes two columns: ~~~text +----------+----------------+ | Sidebar | Main content | | | | | | | +----------+----------------+ ~~~ This is the core idea of responsive design: the structure can remain the same while CSS changes the presentation according to available space. --- ## Testing responsive layouts Browser DevTools includes a device toolbar that lets you simulate different viewport dimensions. You can test common phone and tablet sizes, rotate the viewport, and resize it manually. ~~~callout tip Device mode in the browser In Chrome DevTools press **Ctrl/⌘ + Shift + M** to toggle the device toolbar. Drag the width handle slowly from 320 px upwards and fix the layout wherever it breaks — those are your real breakpoints. ~~~ Manual resizing is particularly useful. Slowly make the viewport narrower and watch for the exact moment when something stops fitting. Look for: - Horizontal scrolling. - Text overlapping other elements. - Navigation becoming too crowded. - Images overflowing their containers. - Buttons becoming difficult to tap. - Excessively long or short text lines. But simulated devices are not enough. Always test important pages on a real phone as well. A real device can reveal differences in touch interaction, font rendering, browser chrome, performance, and how your page feels when used with one hand. Responsive design is ultimately about the experience of a person using the website, not just whether a CSS test passes. --- ## A practical workflow When building a new page, a simple workflow is: 1. Build the semantic HTML structure. 2. Start with the smallest practical viewport. 3. Create a readable single-column layout. 4. Make images fluid. 5. Add a sensible container with `max-width`. 6. Check touch targets and text readability. 7. Increase the viewport until the content naturally needs more space. 8. Add a `min-width` media query. 9. Test intermediate widths, not just predefined device sizes. 10. Test the final page on a real phone. This approach prevents you from treating responsive design as an afterthought. The most important lesson is simple: **do not design for a device; design for the space your content has available.**
takeaways: Responsive design lets one website adapt to many viewport sizes instead of requiring separate device-specific layouts.
Mobile-first CSS starts with the small-screen layout and uses min-width media queries to enhance the design as more space becomes available.
Fluid containers, responsive images, and flexible units help prevent horizontal overflow and make layouts more resilient.
Breakpoints should be chosen when the content needs a layout change, rather than being tied rigidly to particular device models.
DevTools device emulation is useful for testing, but important responsive layouts should also be checked on a real phone.

quiz.question: What does the viewport meta tag with width=device-width primarily tell a mobile browser?
options: To use the device's actual CSS viewport width
To make every element exactly 100px wide
To disable responsive CSS
To force the page into landscape mode
quiz.explanation: width=device-width tells the browser to use the device's actual viewport width for layout calculations.

quiz.question: Which CSS rule is a good default for preventing images from overflowing their containers?
options: img { width: 1200px; }
img { position: fixed; }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }
img { display: none; }
quiz.explanation: max-width: 100% prevents the image from becoming wider than its container, while height: auto preserves its aspect ratio.

quiz.question: In a mobile-first layout, what does a min-width media query normally do?
options: Removes all CSS on large screens
Adds or changes layout rules when the viewport becomes wide enough
Forces every device to use the same width
Makes images load at their largest resolution
quiz.explanation: Mobile-first CSS starts with the small-screen rules and then uses min-width queries to enhance the layout at larger widths.

quiz.question: Why should responsive breakpoints generally be based on content rather than specific devices?
options: Devices cannot have CSS pixels
It prevents JavaScript from running
It guarantees every page has exactly two columns
The layout should change when the content needs more space, regardless of which device provides it
quiz.explanation: Content-based breakpoints make layouts more resilient because they respond to actual layout requirements rather than a fixed list of device models.

quiz.question: What is a useful reason to use clamp() for a heading's font size?
options: It allows the size to scale between a minimum and maximum
It disables text wrapping
It forces the heading to use pixels only
It automatically creates a Grid layout
quiz.explanation: clamp() lets you specify a minimum, preferred flexible value, and maximum, allowing smoother responsive typography.

exercise.title: Make a desktop layout responsive
exercise.task: Convert the provided desktop-only page into a mobile-first responsive layout. The page must include the viewport meta tag, fluid images, a centred container with a maximum width, and a `.columns` section that stacks on small screens. At a suitable `min-width` breakpoint, change `.columns` into a two-column Grid or Flexbox layout. Keep the existing class names because the automated tests use `.container`, `.columns`, and `img`.
